description: Practice on the root centre brings first trembling, then shaking; trembling of hands, feet and head; speech in many tongues; spontaneous mantras and seals; frog-like hopping; leaving the ground (KJN 14.16–19).
With the mind fixed in the heart, samādhi with seizure and possession: the limbs revolve, cries arise (KJN 14.38–39).
In the mind-less state the jīva, dissolved, is not roused even by drums, conches and flutes (KJN 14.85).
In the 'great pervasion', the great sleep, one neither hears nor sees nor smells, fragrant or foul (KJN 17.16–17).
At the end of the twelve a throbbing garland of jewels is seen; the one who sees it is unstained by sin and merit (KJN 13.6; 14.90).
The nectar-principle within the innate is seen throbbing, pure like a jewel, like a pearl or a firefly, sparkling like stars, white, red, black, smoky and yellow (KJN 14.95–96).

Successive attainments: people's affection, freedom from disease, poetry, mastery of speech, far hearing, leaving the ground, meeting the yoginīs, removal of old age, speed, many forms, peace (KJN 7.20–24).
The adamantine body that does not dissolve even at the cosmic dissolution, Bhairava's own claim (KJN 15.22–26).
In breath-control: sweat in the lowest grade, trembling in the middle, rising up in the highest (GŚ 49).
In samādhi the yogī knows no smell, taste, form, touch or sound, neither self nor other, and is not devoured by time (GŚ 97–98).
The body filled with nectar: the seed flows upward and the powers arise; the embodied one does not leave the body (GŚ 65–66).
At the heart centre the 'bull bound threefold' roars loudly (GŚ 60).
Purification of the channels brings kindled fire, manifestation of the inner sound and health (GŚ-Briggs 101).
Kuṇḍalinī seen as a young she-serpent bathed in saffron, coiled three and a half times, asleep facing downward, then rising to the heart where she hears the unstruck sound (Jñāneśvarī 6.221–275).
notes: Lineage given as Vārkarī; Jñāneśvar writes as a Nāth initiate (6.291).

description: By observing lamp-flames in the sixty-four-petalled lotus one sees throughout the body with divine sight (Kulānanda 6–7).

Discrimination, awakening, contentment, joy, thrill, patience, calm, meditation, knowledge, festivity, passion, dispassion, bliss, trembling, swoon and disturbance are listed as forms of nature arising in the practitioner (AmŚ 26).
The guru's forgetting and re-awakening: Matsyendra, entranced in the Kadalī kingdom, recognises himself again at Gorakṣa's drum-words (Gorakṣavijaya).
Gorakṣa's body is said to be unbreakable — a sword rings off it — in the Vīraśaiva accounts of his meeting with Allama (reported by the opposing tradition).
notes: Reported by opponent source (Vīraśaiva Śūnyasampādane / Prabhuliṅgalīle).
